title: Brahma Sūtra

attribution.scholarly: Bādarāyaṇa as final redactor of an older sūtra tradition; identification with Vyāsa not accepted

scholarly.text: c. 2nd c. BCE – 5th c. CE; final redaction often placed c. 400–450 CE

structure.description: 4 adhyāyas × 4 pādas. Śaṅkara's recension: 555 sūtras (pāda counts 31, 32, 43, 28 | 37, 45, 53, 22 | 27, 41, 66, 52 | 19, 21, 16, 22). Other schools divide and number differently: Rāmānuja 545 sūtras, Madhva 564; Nimbārka 549 and Vallabha 554 (these two counts low confidence). Adhikaraṇa counts also differ (Śaṅkara c. 191–192; Rāmānuja c. 156; Madhva c. 223 — low confidence).

editions.name: numerous Devanāgarī editions with Śaṅkara's bhāṣya (e.g. Nirṇaya Sāgara)

notes: Pāda themes (per Śaṅkara): 1.1 texts with clear marks of Brahman; 1.2 unclear marks, Brahman as object of meditation; 1.3 unclear marks, Brahman as object of knowledge; 1.4 doubtful words (avyakta, ajā) claimed by Sāṃkhya; 2.1 objections from smṛti (Sāṃkhya, Yoga) and reason answered; 2.2 critique of Sāṃkhya, Vaiśeṣika, Buddhists, Jains, Pāśupatas and (per Śaṅkara) Pāñcarātra; 2.3 creation of the elements and nature of the jīva; 2.4 the prāṇas; 3.1 transmigration (for dispassion); 3.2 the states of the self and the nature of Brahman; 3.3 combination of meditations; 3.4 auxiliaries of knowledge and the āśramas; 4.1 repetition and the effects of knowledge; 4.2 departure at death; 4.3 the path of the gods; 4.4 the liberated state. All sūtra numbers in this shard follow Śaṅkara's numbering.
summary: Bādarāyaṇa's aphorisms systematizing the Upaniṣads in four adhyāyas — samanvaya (all Upaniṣadic texts converge on Brahman), avirodha (no conflict with smṛti, reason or rival systems, which are critiqued in 2.2), sādhana (transmigration, the states of the self, the meditations, the auxiliaries of knowledge) and phala (repetition of meditation, the knower's freedom from karma, departure, the path of the gods, the liberated state). Every Vedānta school is founded on a commentary on it.

title: Brahmasūtra-vṛtti of Bodhāyana (lost)
notes: Cited at the opening of Rāmānuja's Śrībhāṣya. Some later tradition identifies Bodhāyana with Upavarṣa; not settled.
summary: An extensive commentary (vṛtti) on the Brahma Sūtras, known only from Rāmānuja's statement that earlier teachers abridged it and that he follows it; no manuscript is known.

title: Vṛtti of Upavarṣa on the Mīmāṃsā (lost)
notes: Śaṅkara, BSBh 3.3.53, says the revered Upavarṣa, in the first tantra (Mīmāṃsā), deferred the proof of the self to the Śārīraka; BSBh 1.3.28 cites his view that the letters alone are the word.
summary: A lost commentary covering the Mīmāṃsā sūtras (and, by Śaṅkara's report, promising a treatment of the self in the 'Śārīraka'); known from Śaṅkara's and Śabara's references.

title: Vākya (Chāndogya-vākya) of Brahmanandin/Ṭaṅka (lost)
summary: A lost brief commentary in aphoristic 'sentences' on the Chāndogya Upaniṣad (or on Vedānta generally) by Brahmanandin, also called Ṭaṅka, known from quotations by Yāmuna, Rāmānuja and later writers.

title: Bhāṣya of Dramiḍa on the Vākya (lost)
summary: A lost commentary by Dramiḍa (Draviḍācārya) on Brahmanandin's Vākya, cited by Rāmānuja in the Vedārthasaṅgraha as an authority for a theistic reading of the Upaniṣads.

title: Commentary of Bhartṛprapañca on the Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad (lost)
notes: Known only through opponents' reports (Śaṅkara, Sureśvara, Ānandagiri).
summary: A lost commentary teaching difference-and-non-difference (bhedābheda) and the combination of knowledge and works (jñāna-karma-samuccaya); its views are reported and refuted in Śaṅkara's Bṛhadāraṇyaka commentary and Sureśvara's Vārttika, where Ānandagiri names the author.

title: Māṇḍūkya Kārikā (Gauḍapāda Kārikā, Āgamaśāstra)

attribution.tradition: Gauḍapāda, teacher of Śaṅkara's teacher Govinda; Madhva's school regards the verses of the first prakaraṇa as part of the Upaniṣad (śruti)
attribution.scholarly: Gauḍapāda (c. 6th c.); unity of the four prakaraṇas debated, the fourth sometimes thought an independent work

summary: Gauḍapāda's 215 verses in four prakaraṇas on the Māṇḍūkya Upaniṣad: Āgama (the three states, their three experiencers and the fourth; Oṃ), Vaitathya (the unreality of the waking world, like dream), Advaita (non-duality; the pot-space illustration; asparśa-yoga and the discipline of the mind), and Alātaśānti (the quenching of the firebrand: non-origination, ajātivāda, argued dialectically).

title: Brahmasūtrabhāṣya of Śaṅkara (Śārīrakamīmāṃsābhāṣya)
notes: Sub-commentaries: Padmapāda's Pañcapādikā (→ Prakāśātman's Vivaraṇa), Vācaspati's Bhāmatī (→ Amalānanda's Kalpataru → Appayya's Parimala), Ānandagiri's Nyāyanirṇaya, Govindānanda's Ratnaprabhā.
summary: Śaṅkara's commentary on the Brahma Sūtras, opening with the 'adhyāsa-bhāṣya' on superimposition as the root of all empirical dealings; it reads the sūtras as teaching the non-dual Brahman, the unreality of the world apart from Brahman, knowledge alone as the means to liberation, and liberation while living, and it critiques Sāṃkhya, Vaiśeṣika, the Buddhist schools, the Jains, the Pāśupatas and the Pāñcarātra.

title: Bhagavadgītābhāṣya of Śaṅkara
summary: Śaṅkara's commentary on the Gītā: its introduction distinguishes the Vedic dharma of activity (pravṛtti) and of withdrawal (nivṛtti); it argues at length (introducing 2.11 and 3.1) against the combination of knowledge and works, reads selfless action as purifying the mind for knowledge, and treats knowledge culminating in renunciation as the direct means to liberation.

title: Bṛhadāraṇyakopaniṣadbhāṣya of Śaṅkara
summary: Śaṅkara's longest Upaniṣad commentary; it expounds the self as pure consciousness known through neti neti, the renunciation of the knower and of the seeker, and it refutes Bhartṛprapañca's combination of knowledge and works.

title: Chāndogyopaniṣadbhāṣya of Śaṅkara
summary: Śaṅkara's commentary on the Chāndogya, including the teaching of Uddālaka ('tat tvam asi', ch. 6), the bhūman (ch. 7) and the self of Prajāpati's instruction (ch. 8), and its many meditations (upāsanā).

title: Taittirīyopaniṣadbhāṣya of Śaṅkara
summary: Śaṅkara's commentary, notable for its analysis of 'satyaṃ jñānam anantaṃ brahma' as a definition of Brahman's own nature and for its treatment of the five sheaths.

title: Aitareyopaniṣadbhāṣya of Śaṅkara
summary: Śaṅkara's commentary on the Aitareya, with an introduction arguing that knowledge of the self is for the renunciate and on 'prajñānaṃ brahma'.

title: Īśāvāsyopaniṣadbhāṣya of Śaṅkara
summary: Śaṅkara's commentary distinguishing the path of renunciation in knowledge (verse 1) from the path of works for those unable to renounce (verse 2).

title: Kenopaniṣadbhāṣya of Śaṅkara (pada- and vākya-bhāṣya)
summary: Two commentaries on the Kena, word-by-word and sentence-by-sentence, on Brahman as the unknown knower behind the senses and mind.

title: Kaṭhopaniṣadbhāṣya of Śaṅkara
summary: Śaṅkara's commentary on the Naciketas dialogue, opening with his derivation of the word upaniṣad as knowledge that loosens and destroys the seeds of saṃsāra and leads to Brahman.

title: Praśnopaniṣadbhāṣya of Śaṅkara
summary: Śaṅkara's commentary on the six questions, including meditation on Oṃ and the sixteen-part person.

title: Muṇḍakopaniṣadbhāṣya of Śaṅkara
summary: Śaṅkara's commentary distinguishing the lower (aparā) and higher (parā) knowledge and insisting on approaching a teacher learned in scripture and established in Brahman (1.2.12).

title: Māṇḍūkyopaniṣad-Gauḍapādīyakārikā-bhāṣya (ascribed to Śaṅkara)
notes: Authenticity accepted by most scholars, though some have doubted it.
summary: The commentary on the Māṇḍūkya Upaniṣad together with Gauḍapāda's Kārikā, on the three states and the fourth and on non-origination.

title: Śvetāśvataropaniṣadbhāṣya (ascribed to Śaṅkara)
summary: A commentary on the Śvetāśvatara transmitted under Śaṅkara's name; its authenticity is doubted by modern scholars on grounds of style and citations.

title: Upadeśasāhasrī

attribution.scholarly: accepted as genuine (Hacker, Mayeda)

structure.description: Part I metrical (padya-bandha) 19 chapters; Part II prose (gadya-bandha) 3 chapters (editions differ in which part they print first)

summary: Śaṅkara's independent treatise ('a thousand teachings') in a metrical part (19 chapters) and a prose part (3 chapters): the prose part describes how a teacher should instruct a qualified disciple, gives a model teacher–disciple dialogue, and sets out a meditation (parisaṃkhyāna) on the self as distinct from all objects; the metrical part includes a long chapter on 'tat tvam asi' that rejects the need for repeated meditation (prasaṅkhyāna) after the sentence is understood.

title: Vivekacūḍāmaṇi

attribution.scholarly: attribution to Śaṅkara doubted or rejected by most modern scholars (style, doctrine, citations); probably by later Advaitins of the Śaṅkara tradition

structure.description: c. 580 verses (numbering varies by up to a few verses between editions)

notes: Tradition: Śaṅkara. Hacker, Mayeda and others doubt the attribution; the Śṛṅgeri tradition and most traditional teachers accept it.
summary: A verse manual (c. 580 verses) in dialogue form: the rarity of human birth, the four qualifications, approaching a teacher, the teacher's exposition of the three bodies and five sheaths, the self as witness, māyā and its powers, the three vāsanās, meditation and nirvikalpa samādhi, prārabdha, and the marks of the jīvanmukta.

title: Ātmabodha

attribution.scholarly: attribution to Śaṅkara doubted or rejected by most modern scholars (style, doctrine, citations); probably by later Advaitins of the Śaṅkara tradition

summary: 68 verses for beginners: knowledge alone liberates since action does not oppose ignorance; the self appears as the sheaths as a crystal appears coloured; the three bodies; the world appears real until Brahman, its substratum, is known; meditation and the state of the knower.

title: Aparokṣānubhūti

attribution.scholarly: attribution to Śaṅkara doubted or rejected by most modern scholars (style, doctrine, citations); probably by later Advaitins of the Śaṅkara tradition

summary: 144 verses on direct experience: the four qualifications; inquiry ('who am I? how did this arise?'); the self distinct from the body; and a fifteen-limbed (pañcadaśāṅga) yoga in which yama, niyama, posture, breath control and the rest are reinterpreted as knowledge-disciplines, with a list of the obstacles to samādhi; haṭha is said to be for those whose impurities are not yet burnt.

title: Bhaja Govindam (Mohamudgara)

attribution.scholarly: attribution to Śaṅkara doubted or rejected by most modern scholars (style, doctrine, citations); probably by later Advaitins of the Śaṅkara tradition

structure.description: c. 31 verses in two groups (12 and 14) plus added verses; count varies

summary: A song rebuking attachment and pedantry — 'worship Govinda, you fool; at the time of death grammar rules will not save you' — urging dispassion, good company and worship; tradition says Śaṅkara composed the refrain and first stanzas and his disciples added one each.

title: Nirvāṇaṣaṭkam (Ātmaṣaṭkam)

attribution.scholarly: attribution to Śaṅkara doubted or rejected by most modern scholars (style, doctrine, citations); probably by later Advaitins of the Śaṅkara tradition

summary: Six verses in which the self denies being mind, intellect, ego, the senses, the elements, the breaths, the sheaths, virtue and vice, pleasure and pain, relation and liberation, each ending 'I am of the nature of consciousness and bliss, I am Śiva, I am Śiva'.

title: Dakṣiṇāmūrti Stotram

attribution.scholarly: attribution to Śaṅkara doubted or rejected by most modern scholars (style, doctrine, citations); probably by later Advaitins of the Śaṅkara tradition

summary: Ten verses saluting the guru as Dakṣiṇāmūrti (Śiva as silent teacher): the universe is seen within the self like a city in a mirror, projected outward by māyā as in dream; on waking, one sees the non-dual self. Commented on by Sureśvara's Mānasollāsa.

title: Tattvabodha

attribution.tradition: Śaṅkara; some ascribe it to a later Vāsudevendra
attribution.scholarly: late primer; not by Śaṅkara

summary: A prose primer of Advaita definitions: the four qualifications and six virtues, the three bodies, five sheaths, three states, the twenty-four principles, the creation of the elements, jīva and Īśvara, 'tat tvam asi', the jīvanmukta, and the three kinds of karma and their fate after knowledge.

title: Daśaślokī

attribution.scholarly: attribution to Śaṅkara doubted or rejected by most modern scholars (style, doctrine, citations); probably by later Advaitins of the Śaṅkara tradition

summary: Ten verses each denying that the self is any element, caste, stage or object and ending 'the one that remains, Śiva, the alone, am I'; Madhusūdana's Siddhāntabindu comments on it.

title: Ekaślokī

attribution.scholarly: attribution to Śaṅkara doubted or rejected by most modern scholars (style, doctrine, citations); probably by later Advaitins of the Śaṅkara tradition

summary: A single verse of question and answer on the light by which one sees: sun, lamp, eye, intellect, and finally the self which is the light of lights.

title: Manīṣāpañcaka

attribution.scholarly: attribution to Śaṅkara doubted or rejected by most modern scholars (style, doctrine, citations); probably by later Advaitins of the Śaṅkara tradition

summary: Five verses, set in the tradition's story of Śaṅkara meeting an outcaste (caṇḍāla) at Kāśī, affirming that whoever has firmly realized the one consciousness — outcaste or twice-born — is the guru: 'this is my conviction'.

title: Sādhanapañcaka (Upadeśapañcaka)

attribution.scholarly: attribution to Śaṅkara doubted or rejected by most modern scholars (style, doctrine, citations); probably by later Advaitins of the Śaṅkara tradition

summary: Five verses giving a graded sequence of about forty instructions, from daily Vedic study and duty, through association with the wise and renunciation, to inquiry into the mahāvākya and abiding as Brahman.

title: Kaupīnapañcaka

attribution.scholarly: attribution to Śaṅkara doubted or rejected by most modern scholars (style, doctrine, citations); probably by later Advaitins of the Śaṅkara tradition

summary: Five verses praising the loin-clothed renunciant who delights always in the words of Vedānta, content with alms: 'fortunate indeed are the wearers of the loincloth'.

title: Vākyavṛtti

attribution.scholarly: attribution to Śaṅkara doubted or rejected by most modern scholars (style, doctrine, citations); probably by later Advaitins of the Śaṅkara tradition

summary: A verse treatise explaining the meaning of 'tat tvam asi' by analysing the word-meanings 'that' and 'thou' and the implied identity.

title: Śataślokī

attribution.scholarly: attribution to Śaṅkara doubted or rejected by most modern scholars (style, doctrine, citations); probably by later Advaitins of the Śaṅkara tradition

summary: One hundred verses on Advaita teaching, using many illustrations.

title: Prabodhasudhākara

attribution.scholarly: attribution to Śaṅkara doubted or rejected by most modern scholars (style, doctrine, citations); probably by later Advaitins of the Śaṅkara tradition

summary: A verse treatise combining Advaita teaching with devotion to Kṛṣṇa.

title: Sarvavedāntasiddhāntasārasaṅgraha

attribution.scholarly: attribution to Śaṅkara doubted or rejected by most modern scholars (style, doctrine, citations); probably by later Advaitins of the Śaṅkara tradition

summary: A long verse compendium (c. 1,000 verses) of Advaita doctrine and practice.

title: Pañcīkaraṇa

attribution.scholarly: attribution to Śaṅkara doubted or rejected by most modern scholars (style, doctrine, citations); probably by later Advaitins of the Śaṅkara tradition

summary: A short prose treatise on the quintuplication of the elements, the three bodies and states, and meditation on Oṃ leading to realization of the self; Sureśvara's Vārttika comments on it.

title: Ātmānātmaviveka

attribution.scholarly: attribution to Śaṅkara doubted or rejected by most modern scholars (style, doctrine, citations); probably by later Advaitins of the Śaṅkara tradition

summary: A catechetical prose treatise discriminating the self from the not-self (body, senses, sheaths).

title: Svātmanirūpaṇa

attribution.scholarly: attribution to Śaṅkara doubted or rejected by most modern scholars (style, doctrine, citations); probably by later Advaitins of the Śaṅkara tradition

summary: A verse treatise on the nature of one's own self.

title: Brahmajñānāvalīmālā

attribution.scholarly: attribution to Śaṅkara doubted or rejected by most modern scholars (style, doctrine, citations); probably by later Advaitins of the Śaṅkara tradition

summary: A short verse garland of Brahman-knowledge whose most quoted verse states the 'drum-beat of Vedānta': Brahman is real, the world is false, the jīva is Brahman alone and not other.

title: Dhanyāṣṭaka

attribution.scholarly: attribution to Śaṅkara doubted or rejected by most modern scholars (style, doctrine, citations); probably by later Advaitins of the Śaṅkara tradition

summary: Eight verses on the blessedness of those who have renounced and know the self.

title: Yatipañcaka

attribution.scholarly: attribution to Śaṅkara doubted or rejected by most modern scholars (style, doctrine, citations); probably by later Advaitins of the Śaṅkara tradition

summary: Five verses on the renunciant who abides in the self.

title: Śivānandalaharī

attribution.scholarly: attribution to Śaṅkara doubted or rejected by most modern scholars (style, doctrine, citations); probably by later Advaitins of the Śaṅkara tradition

summary: A hundred devotional verses to Śiva, including the image of devotion as the seed that clings to its tree and the river that flows to the ocean.

title: Maṭhāmnāya (Mahānuśāsana, Maṭhāmnāya-setu)

attribution.scholarly: a late maṭha document; versions differ between maṭhas

summary: A short text, transmitted in the Daśanāmī maṭhas and ascribed to Śaṅkara, assigning to each of the four āmnāya maṭhas its direction, Veda, mahāvākya, presiding deities, first ācārya, and the sannyāsa names attached to it; it is the tradition's charter for the order.

title: Hastāmalakīya (Hastāmalaka-stotra)
summary: Twelve (or fourteen) verses ascribed to Hastāmalaka, answering Śaṅkara's question 'who are you?' by declaring himself the eternal consciousness that, like the sun, illumines mind and senses; a commentary is ascribed to Śaṅkara.

title: Toṭakāṣṭaka
summary: Eight verses in the toṭaka metre in praise of Śaṅkara as guru ('bhava śaṅkara deśika me śaraṇam'), ascribed to his disciple Toṭaka.

title: Śrutisārasamuddharaṇa
summary: A verse treatise by Toṭaka drawing out 'the essence of the Upaniṣads' in dialogue form: the self as witness distinct from the not-self, and the meaning of the mahāvākyas.

title: Naiṣkarmyasiddhi
summary: Sureśvara's treatise (verse with prose) establishing 'actionlessness': ch. 1 refutes the view that works, alone or combined with knowledge, lead to liberation; ch. 2 separates the self from the not-self by agreement and difference; ch. 3 explains how 'tat tvam asi' gives immediate knowledge; ch. 4 summarizes and describes the knower, whose virtues arise without effort and who cannot act licentiously.

title: Bṛhadāraṇyakopaniṣadbhāṣyavārttika
summary: Sureśvara's massive verse sub-commentary on Śaṅkara's Bṛhadāraṇyaka commentary; source of the semblance theory (ābhāsa-vāda) of the jīva, of the principle that any method (prakriyā) that leads to knowledge of the inner self is valid, and of a detailed refutation of Bhartṛprapañca.

title: Taittirīyopaniṣadbhāṣyavārttika
summary: Sureśvara's verse sub-commentary on Śaṅkara's Taittirīya commentary, including the sheaths and the definition of Brahman.

title: Mānasollāsa
summary: A verse commentary on the Dakṣiṇāmūrti Stotram ascribed to Sureśvara, explaining it through the three states and the witness.

title: Pañcīkaraṇavārttika
summary: A verse commentary on the Pañcīkaraṇa ascribed to Sureśvara.

title: Brahmasiddhi
notes: Commentaries: Vācaspati's Tattvasamīkṣā (lost), Citsukha's Abhiprāyaprakāśikā, Ānandapūrṇa's Bhāvaśuddhi, Śaṅkhapāṇi's vyākhyā (last three low confidence).
summary: Maṇḍana Miśra's independent Advaita treatise in four chapters (Brahma-, Tarka-, Niyoga-, Siddhi-kāṇḍa): Brahman as bliss and consciousness; avidyā residing in the individual selves as non-apprehension and misapprehension; perception grasps being, not difference; critique of the view that the Upaniṣads enjoin (niyoga); liberation through knowledge made direct by repeated contemplation (prasaṅkhyāna), with works as helpful.

title: Vibhramaviveka
summary: Maṇḍana Miśra's short verse treatise examining the theories of perceptual error (khyāti) of the rival schools.

title: Pañcapādikā

attribution.tradition: Padmapāda; the name 'five pādas' and the tradition that the rest was destroyed (his uncle burnt the manuscript, Śaṅkaradigvijaya) explain why only the opening survives
attribution.scholarly: Padmapāda (8th c.)

summary: Padmapāda's commentary on the adhyāsa-bhāṣya and the first four sūtras of Śaṅkara's BSBh: analyses the definition of superimposition, presents ignorance as an insentient power (avidyā-śakti) that is the material cause of superimposition, glosses 'mithyā' as 'indescribable', and treats the jīva as a reflection of Brahman in the ego.

title: Pañcapādikāvivaraṇa
summary: Prakāśātman's sub-commentary on the Pañcapādikā, founding text of the Vivaraṇa school: Brahman is the locus and object of a positive (bhāva-rūpa) indescribable ignorance, established by perception, inference and presumption; the jīva is the reflection of Brahman, real and identical with its prototype; hearing is the principal means, enjoined by a restrictive injunction; the mahāvākya yields immediate knowledge.

title: Tattvadīpana
summary: Akhaṇḍānanda's sub-commentary on the Pañcapādikāvivaraṇa.

title: Vivaraṇaprameyasaṅgraha
summary: Vidyāraṇya's independent exposition of the doctrines (prameya) of the Vivaraṇa, arranged by topics rather than as a line-by-line gloss.

title: Bhāmatī

attribution.tradition: Vācaspati Miśra; named after his wife Bhāmatī, who served him through the years of its writing
attribution.scholarly: Vācaspati Miśra

scholarly.text: 9th or 10th c. CE (depending on reading the date of his Nyāyasūcīnibandha, 898, as Vikrama = 841 CE or Śaka = 976 CE)

summary: Vācaspati Miśra's commentary on the whole of Śaṅkara's BSBh, named (tradition) after his wife; founding text of the Bhāmatī school: ignorance resides in the jīvas with Brahman as its object; the jīva is Brahman delimited by the inner organ; the mahāvākya gives mediate knowledge which the mind, perfected by contemplation, makes direct; works generate the desire to know. It follows Maṇḍana on several points.

title: Tattvasamīkṣā (lost)
summary: Vācaspati Miśra's commentary on Maṇḍana's Brahmasiddhi, referred to in his other works; not extant.

title: Vedāntakalpataru
summary: Amalānanda's sub-commentary on the Bhāmatī, defending and extending its positions.

title: Śāstradarpaṇa
summary: Amalānanda's independent work summarizing the adhikaraṇas of the Brahma Sūtras in the Bhāmatī line.

title: Kalpataruparimala
summary: Appayya Dīkṣita's commentary on the Vedāntakalpataru, completing the Bhāmatī commentarial chain.

title: Siddhāntaleśasaṅgraha
summary: Appayya Dīkṣita's compendium, in four chapters, of the divergent views held by Advaita teachers on the locus of ignorance, the nature of Īśvara and the jīva (limitation, reflection, semblance, one-jīva), the means of knowledge, the role of works and of hearing, and liberation, prefaced by the principle that the ancients, intent only on the oneness of the self, were indifferent to how the empirical is explained.

title: Nyāyarakṣāmaṇi
summary: Appayya Dīkṣita's Advaita commentary on the adhikaraṇas of the first pāda(s) of the Brahma Sūtras.

title: Saṃkṣepaśārīraka

tradition.text: Sarvajñātman is held to be the disciple of Sureśvara ('Deveśvara')

summary: Sarvajñātman's verse summary (four chapters) of the teaching of Śaṅkara's BSBh: pure, partless consciousness alone is both the locus and object of ignorance; Īśvara and jīva as reflections; the scriptural statements of creation as provisional superimposition.

title: Pañcaprakriyā
summary: A short work by Sarvajñātman on five topics of Advaita method.

title: Iṣṭasiddhi
summary: Vimuktātman's treatise establishing the 'desired' (iṣṭa) conclusion that the self is pure experience (anubhūti) and that ignorance and its products are indescribable (anirvacanīya), with a critique of the rival theories of error in favour of indescribability.

title: Nyāyamakaranda
summary: Ānandabodha's dialectical treatise defending the self-luminosity of the self, indescribable ignorance and the falsity of difference; Citsukha commented on it.

title: Khaṇḍanakhaṇḍakhādya

scholarly.text: 12th c. CE (court of Jayacandra of Kanauj)

summary: Śrīharṣa's 'sweets of refutation': a dialectical work (four chapters) that refutes, one after another, the definitions of cognition, valid cognition, the means of knowledge and the categories given by the Naiyāyikas, showing that nothing other than self-luminous consciousness can be defined; the Advaitin may debate on the basis of what the opponent accepts without committing to the reality of the categories.

title: Tattvapradīpikā (Citsukhī)
summary: Citsukha's dialectical treatise (four chapters): defines self-luminosity as 'being fit for immediate usage while not being an object of cognition', proves the self self-luminous, defends indescribable ignorance, refutes Nyāya's categories and defines falsity as being the counterpositive of an absolute absence in its own locus.

title: Nyāyanirṇaya
summary: Ānandagiri's gloss on Śaṅkara's BSBh; Ānandagiri also glossed Śaṅkara's Upaniṣad and Gītā commentaries.

title: Ratnaprabhā
summary: Govindānanda's widely used explanatory gloss on Śaṅkara's BSBh.

title: Pañcadaśī

attribution.tradition: Vidyāraṇya; some accounts ascribe part of the work to Bhāratītīrtha
attribution.scholarly: Vidyāraṇya (with possible co-authorship)

structure.description: 15 chapters in three groups of five

summary: Vidyāraṇya's fifteen-chapter verse manual in three pentads — five 'discriminations' (viveka: of reality, the elements, the sheaths, duality, the great sayings), five 'lamps' (dīpa: the picture, contentment, the immutable, meditation, the theatre) and five 'blisses' (ānanda: of yoga, of the self, of non-duality, of knowledge, of objects). It distinguishes māyā (pure sattva) as the adjunct of Īśvara from avidyā (impure sattva) as the adjunct of the jīva, and gives the canvas, four-space, tenth-man and theatre-lamp illustrations and the seven states of the jīva.

title: Jīvanmuktiviveka
summary: Vidyāraṇya's treatise on liberation while living in five chapters: scriptural proof and the two kinds of renunciation (of the seeker, vividiṣā; of the knower, vidvat); the destruction of latent tendencies (vāsanā-kṣaya); the dissolution of the mind (mano-nāśa); the five purposes of jīvanmukti; and the life of the paramahaṃsa. It draws heavily on the Yoga Vāsiṣṭha.

title: Anubhūtiprakāśa
summary: Vidyāraṇya's verse exposition of the teaching of the principal Upaniṣads.

title: Vaiyāsikanyāyamālā
summary: A verse summary of the adhikaraṇas of the Brahma Sūtras (Advaita reading) ascribed to Bhāratītīrtha.

title: Dṛg-Dṛśya Viveka (Vākyasudhā)

attribution.scholarly: probably 14th c., Bhāratītīrtha or Vidyāraṇya

summary: 46 verses discriminating the seer from the seen: form is seen by the eye, the eye by the mind, the mind's states by the witness, which is never seen; the two powers of māyā; the five aspects of every thing (is, shines, dear; name, form); six kinds of samādhi; three kinds of jīva.

title: Śaṅkaradigvijaya (Mādhavīya)

attribution.scholarly: a later compilation (c. 17th–18th c.) drawing on earlier Śaṅkaravijayas

notes: Other hagiographies (not separately entered): Anantānandagiri's Śaṅkaravijaya, Cidvilāsa's Śaṅkaravijayavilāsa, Vyāsācala's Śaṅkaravijaya, Rājacūḍāmaṇi Dīkṣita's Śaṅkarābhyudaya; the Kāñcī tradition also cites a Bṛhat-Śaṅkaravijaya. Accounts differ on Śaṅkara's place of passing (Kedāra; Kāñcī).
summary: The most widely read hagiography of Śaṅkara (16 cantos): birth at Kālaṭi, renunciation, discipleship under Govinda, the meeting with Vyāsa, Kumārila on the pyre, the debate with Maṇḍana judged by Ubhaya Bhāratī, the disciples, the conquest of the quarters and the Sarvajña-pīṭha, and his departure.

title: Sarvadarśanasaṅgraha

attribution.scholarly: a Mādhava of the 14th c.; identity with Vidyāraṇya debated

summary: A doxography of sixteen systems, from the Cārvāka through the Buddhist, Jain, Vaiṣṇava, Śaiva, Nyāya, Mīmāṃsā, grammatical, Sāṃkhya and Yoga schools, each refuted by the next, ending with (a reference to) Advaita as the culmination.

title: Vedāntasiddhāntamuktāvalī
summary: Prakāśānanda's treatise arguing that the world exists only in being perceived (dṛṣṭi-sṛṣṭi-vāda), that there is one jīva (eka-jīva-vāda), and that ignorance alone accounts for the appearance, with no need of a theory of creation.

title: Advaitasiddhi
notes: The debate continued: Rāmācārya's Taraṅgiṇī (Dvaita) answered it; Brahmānanda Sarasvatī's Laghucandrikā (Gauḍa-Brahmānandī) replied to the Taraṅgiṇī.
summary: Madhusūdana Sarasvatī's great dialectical defence of Advaita (four chapters) against Vyāsatīrtha's Nyāyāmṛta, answering it point by point in Navya-Nyāya language: the falsity (mithyātva) of the world under five definitions, the inference 'the world is false because it is seen, insentient and limited', indescribable ignorance, the partless meaning of the mahāvākya, the means and liberation.

title: Gūḍhārthadīpikā
summary: Madhusūdana Sarasvatī's commentary on the Bhagavad Gītā, reading its three hexads as the sections on works, devotion/meditation and knowledge, and joining Advaita with an intense devotion to Kṛṣṇa.

title: Siddhāntabindu
summary: Madhusūdana's commentary on the Daśaślokī, a compact survey of Advaita doctrine including the theories of the jīva and Īśvara.

title: Bhaktirasāyana
summary: Madhusūdana's treatise (three chapters) on devotion as a rasa: devotion is a mental mode that, the mind having melted through hearing of the Lord's qualities, flows continuously toward the Lord; it is a supreme human goal in its own right.

title: Vedāntakalpalatikā
summary: Madhusūdana's early treatise on liberation and its means, surveying and refuting other schools' conceptions of liberation.

title: Advaitaratnarakṣaṇa
summary: Madhusūdana's defence of Advaita against dualist (Nyāya and Vaiṣṇava) objections, on the authority of scripture for non-difference.

title: Prasthānabheda
summary: Madhusūdana's classification of the branches of learning (Vedas, Vedāṅgas, darśanas, Purāṇas, arts) as all converging, directly or indirectly, on the Lord and on Advaita.

title: Laghucandrikā (Gauḍabrahmānandī)
summary: Brahmānanda Sarasvatī's commentary on the Advaitasiddhi, answering the Dvaita reply (Taraṅgiṇī).

title: Vedāntasāra
notes: Commentaries: Nṛsiṃha Sarasvatī's Subodhinī (1588), Rāmatīrtha's Vidvanmanorañjanī.
summary: Sadānanda's standard primer: the four preliminaries (qualified student, subject, relation, purpose); superimposition and retraction; ignorance with its two powers, collective and individual, and the three bodies, states and sheaths; quintuplication; a graded refutation of mistaken views of the self; the analysis of 'tat tvam asi' by exclusive-inclusive implication; hearing, reflection, contemplation and samādhi with eight auxiliaries and four obstacles; the jīvanmukta.

title: Subodhinī (on the Vedāntasāra)
summary: Nṛsiṃha Sarasvatī's commentary on the Vedāntasāra (dated 1588 CE in its colophon, low confidence).

title: Vidvanmanorañjanī
summary: Rāmatīrtha's commentary on the Vedāntasāra.

title: Vedāntaparibhāṣā
summary: Dharmarāja Adhvarīndra's manual of Advaita epistemology in eight chapters: perception, inference, comparison, verbal testimony, presumption and non-cognition (the six means of knowledge, following Bhāṭṭa Mīmāṃsā for empirical matters), then the object (Brahman's defining marks, creation and dissolution) and the purpose (liberation and its means).

title: Śikhāmaṇi
summary: Rāmakṛṣṇa Adhvarin's commentary on his father Dharmarāja's Vedāntaparibhāṣā.

title: Advaitamakaranda
summary: Lakṣmīdhara Kavi's short verse treatise (c. 28 verses) on the self as existence, consciousness and bliss, the witness of all.

title: Vedāntatattvaviveka
summary: Nṛsiṃhāśrama's treatise on the principal topics of Advaita in the Vivaraṇa manner.

title: Ātmapurāṇa
summary: Śaṅkarānanda's long verse retelling of the teaching of the Upaniṣads in narrative form.

title: Svārājyasiddhi
summary: Gaṅgādharendra Sarasvatī's verse treatise (with auto-commentary) on attaining 'self-sovereignty' — liberation as the self's rule over itself.

title: Ātmavidyāvilāsa
summary: Sadāśiva Brahmendra's verses on the conduct and inner state of the avadhūta knower of the self.

title: Advaitabodhadīpikā
summary: A late catechetical Advaita treatise attributed to Karapātra Svāmī, known through its Tamil rendering in Ramaṇa Maharṣi's circle.

title: Kaivalya Navanītam
summary: A Tamil verse classic of Advaita by Tāṇḍavarāya Svāmī in two parts (exposition of the truth; clearing of doubts), teacher–disciple in form.

title: Tripura Rahasya (Jñāna-khaṇḍa)

attribution.tradition: narrated by Haritāyana, conveying Dattātreya's teaching to Paraśurāma
attribution.scholarly: a late (c. 13th–17th c.) Śrīvidyā-milieu text; date uncertain

structure.description: Māhātmya and Jñāna khaṇḍas survive (a Caryā khaṇḍa is said to be lost); the Jñāna-khaṇḍa has c. 22 chapters (low confidence)

notes: Its non-dualism of self-aware consciousness is closer to Śākta/Pratyabhijñā thought than to Śaṅkara's; placed under Advaita by the registry and by modern Advaita use (e.g. Ramaṇa's circle).
summary: A Śākta-Advaita teaching in verse in which Dattātreya instructs Paraśurāma, narrated by Haritāyana; through stories such as that of Hemacūḍa taught by his wife Hemalekhā it teaches that the self is consciousness that knows itself (with the power of self-awareness, vimarśa), that the world is its reflection like an image in a mirror, and that realization is stable abidance beyond the alternation of samādhi and activity.

title: Bhāvārthadīpikā
summary: Śrīdhara Svāmin's commentary on the Bhāgavata Purāṇa, combining an Advaita frame with devotion to the Lord; authoritative for many later Vaiṣṇava schools.

title: Mūlāvidyānirāsa
summary: Swami Satchidanandendra Sarasvati's (recent) Sanskrit polemic arguing that Śaṅkara did not teach a positive root-ignorance (mūlāvidyā) and that the Vivaraṇa and later schools depart from him.

title: Vidhiviveka
summary: Maṇḍana Miśra's Mīmāṃsā treatise on the nature of Vedic injunction (vidhi), commented on by Vācaspati's Nyāyakaṇikā.

title: Bhāvanāviveka
summary: Maṇḍana Miśra's Mīmāṃsā treatise on bhāvanā, the productive force expressed by the verb in injunctions.

title: Sphoṭasiddhi
summary: Maṇḍana Miśra's defence of the grammarians' doctrine of sphoṭa (the meaning-bearing word-whole) against Mīmāṃsā objections.

title: Śivārkamaṇidīpikā
summary: Appayya Dīkṣita's commentary on Śrīkaṇṭha's Brahmasūtra-bhāṣya (Śaiva Vedānta), written from the standpoint of a Śiva devotee.
